doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

chapter: Radio, the Jazz Institute and Kenton
title: Programming for radio versus the Jazz Institute
summary: Poston traces KLON, the Los Angeles Jazz Institute and KSDS, and says radio events must be unique rather than compete with local promoters.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Yeah. And how do you take the pulse of the Southern California area to try to program the acts and the artists that will bring those people? Is it partly your radio work or word of mouth?

It depends what it is and what we’re doing because kind of the sequence of events for me was what used to be KLON Radio in Long Beach, which now is K-JAZZ, so I was there for 13 or 14 years producing concerts and festivals and on the air as well. Then the Los Angeles Jazz Institute, which I still operate the Jazz Institute, but then almost ten years ago now I became the general manager at KSDS in San Diego because I truly wanted to see jazz radio continue. And I decided I could continue to do all the other things I did as well as run the radio station so all of those things as far as — they have different approaches. Like for the radio station when we do events there’s usually a concept or a reason why we’re doing it. Because I’ve never felt as a radio station that our role is to compete with other area promoters who are struggling too — whether it’s clubs or festivals or whatever. So I’ve always felt with the radio station aspect that what we do there has to be something very unique, very special, or has to have some unique aspect of it. That’s why I’ve rarely — I say rarely but I guess in percentage-wise — I’m usually not in a position where I’m just hiring a set group to play for an occasion. I’m usually having to create something, and put something together whether it be a reunion of sorts or whether it be putting a band together to play someone’s arrangements — whatever the case may be, that’s always been more of the direction, especially with radio. Because © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

again, you know there’s — our job with radio is to promote what the local promoters are doing, to try to help them, not to compete against them. So we do things — again — for a purpose. Sometimes the purpose is as a fundraiser for the radio station. Sometimes it’s to showcase something or an artist or maybe to celebrate a historical occasion or to celebrate something — a new release, or whatever the case may be. Jazz Institute is a little bit different in that the archive is the centerpiece of the Jazz Institute. And this large archive that we’ve built over the years, that has many artist collections — most of which are Southern California related. I knew from working with all the artists, and when we started this, that the idea was that a lot of them complained about donating their materials to a place where they’re going to be locked away and never heard from again. And I knew that ideally what Pete Rugolo and Shorty Rogers and Bud Shank and some guys like that, what they wanted really, even if they wouldn’t come right out and say it, was that their legacy would continue after they were gone. So we decided with the Jazz Institute where the archive would be the centerpiece and then the events and the festivals and things that we did would all utilize materials in the archive to be able to showcase and maintain those legacies. And for the first several years when we were doing it, many of the musicians were still alive. Now that’s not the case now — we’re just about out of a lot of the musicians of the eras that these collections represent. But we’ve been able to utilize the music, by doing concerts of their music, we’ve been able to utilize the recordings by doing a series of CD reissues of rare materials, things like that. Now I can — obviously I marry the two together so I can incorporate some of those things now into the radio element as well, but then also all those events always were multi-day — or I should say are, not was — panel discussions, film showings, utilizing the films, presentations that utilize photographs and memorabilia and audio and so on. So that’s been our focus with the Jazz Institute is to really utilize these materials and keep them a living, breathing thing, and not just lock them away. Because the amount of researchers, and you know you get a fair amount of serious researchers that are doing things and that’s great, but still to me to keep those things alive. And then they become natural fundraisers for the institute that way because theoretically you’re raising money from doing the events. So the radio purposes are related but a little bit different and then the institute archive purposes are a little bit different in approach, but they each have their own reasons as to why we do things.
